We need to propose a retrosynthesis route (max 3 steps) to target SMILES: Cc1ccc(NS(=O)(=O)c2ccc(/C=C/C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N)cc2)cc1

We have a template (733) that disassembles sulfonamide into aryl chloride sulfonyl chloride and an aniline. The retro template: product (sulfonamide) -> Cl-SO2-aryl + NH2-aryl. So we can break the sulfonamide bond.

Our target has a sulfonamide linking two aryl rings: left ring is p-tolyl (CH3 on phenyl) attached to N of sulfonamide; right ring is phenyl with a side chain: /C=C/C(=O)N-phenyl-N (anilide). Actually the right aryl is phenyl bearing the side chain (trans-α,β-unsaturated amide attached to an aniline). The sulfonamide attaches to that phenyl at para position.

Thus retrosynthesis step 1: break sulfonamide using template 733 to give two precursors:

- Aryl chloride sulfonyl chloride? Actually the retro template gives Cl-SO2-aryl (aryl sulfonyl chloride) and NH2-aryl (aniline). The product is sulfonamide linking aryls. So precursors: aryl sulfonyl chloride (Cl-SO2-aryl) where aryl is the right phenyl (the one bearing side chain). And aniline (NH2-aryl) where aryl is left tolyl.

Specifically:

Precursor A: Cl-S(=O)(=O)-c2ccc(/C=C/C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N)cc2 (aryl sulfonyl chloride)

Precursor B: Aniline: Cc1ccc(N)cc1 (p-toluidine)

Check buyability: we already checked p-toluidine is buyable (True). The sulfonyl chloride maybe not buyable (False). Need to find commercially available sulfonyl chloride that matches. Could we use a simpler sulfonyl chloride and then later functionalize? But we have max 3 steps. Maybe we can use a sulfonyl chloride that is commercially available and then do a substitution to attach the side chain later (via Suzuki? but side chain is attached to aryl via a vinyl amide). Could we instead break the amide later? Another approach: break amide first, then sulfonamide.

Let's consider stepwise: target -> break amide (C=O)N-aryl (anilide) using amide formation template? There may be a template for amide formation (reverse of amide). Search for amide formation (functional_groups_formed: amide). The earlier search gave many templates but not sure.

But we could break the amide to give an acid (or acid chloride) and an aniline. The side chain is /C=C/C(=O)N-Ph-NH2? Actually the side chain is C=O attached to N attached to phenyl with an NH (aniline). The amide is between the α,β-unsaturated carbonyl and an aniline (Nc3ccccc3N). So the amide attaches to an aniline that also has an NH2 (para? Actually Nc3ccccc3N is an aniline with an NH2 at para? The SMILES: Nc3ccccc3N means an aniline with two amino groups? Wait: c3ccccc3 is phenyl; preceding N is attached to carbonyl (amide N). After that N attached to phenyl? Actually "Nc3ccccc3N" means N attached to phenyl at position 1, and phenyl has an N substituent at position? The SMILES: N c3 c c c c c3 N. That is an aniline with an amino group at the other end? So it's a phenyl diamine (p-phenylenediamine) where one NH is part of amide, the other is free NH2.

Thus the right aryl is a phenyl with two amino groups: one amide, one free NH2. The sulfonamide attaches to that phenyl at para to the amide? Actually the sulfonamide attaches to the phenyl at position para to the amide? The SMILES: c2ccc(/C=C/C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N)cc2. So the phenyl (c2ccc...cc2) has the side chain at one position, and the sulfonamide attaches at the same phenyl (the sulfonyl group attaches to that phenyl). So the phenyl has both sulfonyl and side chain substituents.

Thus breaking sulfonamide gives sulfonyl chloride attached to that phenyl (still bearing side chain). That sulfonyl chloride may not be commercially available. Could we instead break the amide first to give a simpler aryl sulfonamide? Not sure.

Alternative: Use sulfonyl chloride that is commercially available (e.g., p-toluenesulfonyl chloride) and then attach the right aryl via nucleophilic aromatic substitution? Not feasible.

Maybe we can break the sulfonamide to give p-toluidine (buyable) and aryl sulfonyl chloride (maybe not buyable). Could we find a commercially available aryl sulfonyl chloride that matches? Search.
